summary: This work demonstrates break-even performance of a noise-adapted 3-qubit probabilistic quantum error correction code on IBM superconducting qubits, achieving logical qubit lifetimes of ~740 µs compared to bare qubit T₁ ~ 220 µs. The scheme combines hardware-efficient variational circuits for encoding/recovery, dynamical decoupling (CHaDD) to suppress crosstalk dephasing, and introduces a gain metric accounting for post-selection overhead.
motivation: Conventional QEC schemes require prohibitive resources (e.g., surface codes need 17 qubits per logical qubit), while noise-adapted approaches tailored to dominant hardware noise can be more practical on NISQ devices. Demonstrating logical qubit lifetimes exceeding physical qubit relaxation times with only 5 total qubits would validate this noise-engineered approach.
method: A 3-qubit Dicke-state code encoding permutation-invariant states ($|0_L\rangle = (|100\rangle + |010\rangle + |001\rangle)/\sqrt{3}$, $|1_L\rangle = |111\rangle$) was implemented on IBM Torino using variational quantum circuits to construct hardware-efficient encoders and approximate recovery circuits (setting $\gamma = 0$ in recovery operators to reduce depth from 60+ to 5 CZ gates). Multi-round QEC with 30 µs intervals and interleaved chromatic Hadamard DD (CHaDD) mitigated crosstalk; post-selection quantified via a signal-to-noise ratio gain metric.
result: Multiple logical qubits demonstrated $T_1$ lifetimes exceeding physical qubits by 3.4×; $|0_L\rangle$ and $|1_L\rangle$ fidelities surpassed bare qubit decay across evolution times up to ~200 µs. Measurement readout fidelity ($\sim 10^{-2}$) emerged as the primary performance bottleneck; gain reached near-unity in certain regimes. Simulations predict significant improvement with sub-1% readout errors on future devices.
